\section{Extended Related Work}
\label{app:related_work}

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 1: Grammar-Constrained Decoding
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Grammar-Constrained Decoding.}
Recent work has established efficient algorithms for restricting LLM outputs to conform to context-free grammars, making grammar-constrained decoding the de facto standard for obtaining structured output from language models.
XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar} partitions the vocabulary into context-independent and context-dependent tokens and maintains persistent pushdown automata across decoding steps, achieving up to 100$\times$ speedup over prior CFG-constrained decoding methods.
Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines} reformulates constrained generation as finite-state machine transitions with offline vocabulary indexing, which enables efficient enforcement of regular-expression and JSON-schema constraints without runtime overhead per token.
LMQL~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql} introduces a declarative query language that compiles type, length, and regex constraints into token-level masks, providing a programmable interface for specifying multi-variable output structures.
These systems ensure that every generated token belongs to a grammar-valid continuation, but they do not address the \emph{distribution distortion} introduced by naive token masking.
A parallel line of work tackles this problem directly: DOMINO~\cite{beurer-kellner2024domino} minimizes distributional divergence during CFG enforcement by formulating mask selection as an optimization problem, and ASAp~\cite{park2024grammar} provides a provably unbiased sampling algorithm that preserves the original LM distribution under grammar constraints.
Together, these advances have made grammar-constrained decoding both fast and statistically principled, and provide a robust foundation for structured generation.
However, all of these methods operate exclusively at the syntactic level: they ensure format validity (e.g., well-formed JSON, valid enum values) but cannot enforce cross-field semantic constraints such as ontology domain/range rules that depend on previously generated content.
This syntactic-only limitation motivates OntoCoDec's semantic extension: our grammar layer builds on XGrammar for structural (JSON schema and enum) constraints, while a second semantic layer enforces relational type constraints that are inherently beyond the expressive power of context-free grammars.

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 1.5: Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code.}
In programming-language generation, constrained decoding has been extended beyond syntax to enforce semantic properties such as type correctness; this work demonstrates that richer-than-CFG constraints can be compiled into token-level filtering.
In the text-to-SQL domain, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} maintains an incremental SQL parsing state that rejects tokens violating syntax or referencing non-existent database columns at each decoding step, achieving state-of-the-art results on Spider and CoSQL without modifying model weights.
While mechanistically similar to OntoCoDec's token-level filtering, PICARD operates over a \emph{fixed, fully enumerated} schema (database table and column names known before decoding begins).
In contrast, OntoCoDec's entity registry is populated \emph{during} generation as entity spans are extracted from free text; constraint sets evolve with the decoding prefix, a fundamental distinction between querying a known schema and extracting from unstructured text.
Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022} pioneers Constrained Semantic Decoding (CSD), which enforces syntax, type, and scope constraints simultaneously during code generation from pre-trained LMs without fine-tuning; this establishes that semantic constraints can be expressed as dynamic token masks conditioned on the generation prefix.
MGD~\cite{mgd_neurips2023} uses static-analysis monitors to perform incremental type checking at decode time; SantaCoder-1.1B with MGD outperforms text-davinci-003 on repository-level code completion by ensuring that every generated identifier is type-correct with respect to the surrounding code context.
Most recently, \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile full type systems, including generic types and subtyping, into prefix automata for token-level logits masking and reduce compilation errors by over 50\%.
This last system is the closest mechanistic analog to OntoCoDec, applying the same ``type system $\to$ automaton $\to$ logits mask'' pipeline, though in a fundamentally different domain.
The key technical difference lies in the constraint structure: programming-language type systems feature deep subtyping hierarchies and parametric polymorphism, whereas IE ontology axioms specify flat domain/range sets; a relation $R$ accepts head entities from set $\mathcal{D}(R)$ and tail entities from set $\mathcal{R}(R)$, with no subtype chains.
Conversely, IE introduces a challenge absent in code generation: the constraint target (entity type) must be inferred from free-text spans rather than read from declared type annotations, so a stateful entity registry must track extracted types during autoregressive generation.
These methods collectively demonstrate that semantic (type) constraints at decode time are both feasible and highly effective, but exclusively in the code domain where type systems are formally specified.
OntoCoDec is the first to \emph{automatically compile} IE ontology axioms, including domain/range constraints, into token-level decoding masks for information extraction, migrating the type-constrained decoding paradigm from code generation to IE.

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 2: Vocabulary/Type-Constrained Generation
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Vocabulary and Type-Constrained Generation.}
The idea of enforcing entity-type compatibility constraints for information extraction dates back to pre-neural methods.
\citet{roth_yih_2004} formulate joint entity and relation identification as an integer linear program (ILP) that enforces type constraints (e.g., \textsc{Emp-Org} only between \textsc{Per} and \textsc{Org} entities); this establishes the foundational principle that relational type compatibility should be a hard constraint, not a soft preference learned from data.
In the autoregressive era, GENRE~\cite{decao2021genre} pioneers trie-based constrained beam search for autoregressive entity retrieval, restricting each decoding step to tokens consistent with valid entity names from a predefined catalog.
GenIE~\cite{josifoski2022genie} extends this approach to end-to-end information extraction with state-based constraints that enforce valid triple structures, achieving strong performance on closed-world knowledge base population, though it requires task-specific fine-tuning on the target schema.
AdaKGC~\cite{adakgc_emnlp2023} introduces schema-constrained dynamic decoding with trie-based prefix trees that adapt to the target schema, enforcing that generated entity and relation names belong to a predefined inventory, a vocabulary-level constraint that ensures name validity but does not verify type compatibility between a relation and its arguments.
GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} provides a unified grammar-constrained decoding framework for structured NLP tasks including IE, introducing input-dependent grammars that adapt constraints based on the source text. GCD is the closest precursor to OntoCoDec in applying logits masking to IE, though limited to syntactic constraints.
NeuroLogic Decoding~\cite{lu2021neurologic} expresses lexical inclusion and exclusion constraints as predicate logic formulas enforced during beam search, offering a general mechanism for token-level control that can encode vocabulary membership but not relational type rules.
These approaches constrain \emph{which tokens} can appear (vocabulary membership) but not \emph{which type combinations} are valid for a given relation.
OntoCoDec's semantic layer enforces relational constraints (e.g., that the head entity of relation $R$ must belong to type set $\mathcal{D}(R)$) which cannot be expressed as static vocabulary restrictions because the valid set depends on the relation type generated earlier in the same sequence.
While Roth \& Yih's ILP formulation shares the same type-compatibility motivation, it operates as a post-hoc reranker over discrete candidates; OntoCoDec integrates enforcement directly into autoregressive decoding, preventing violations rather than filtering them.

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 3: Structural Constraints for IE
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Structural Constraints via Training and Prompting.}
An orthogonal approach encodes IE output structure through model training or prompt design rather than decoding-time enforcement, relying on learned representations to produce schema-compliant outputs.
UIE~\cite{lu2022uie} defines a Structured Extraction Language and trains a unified text-to-structure model across 13 IE datasets, relying on large-scale pre-training to internalize output format constraints.
GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} expresses annotation guidelines as Python dataclass definitions and fine-tunes Code-LLaMA to generate typed code, achieving strong zero-shot transfer to unseen IE schemas through the implicit type structure of programming languages.
KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} takes this further by encoding 29K entity types from Wikidata as a Python class hierarchy, training a Code-LLM to generate structured extraction code that implicitly respects type inheritance, the most comprehensive schema-as-code approach to date.
CodeIE~\cite{li2023codeie} similarly reformulates IE as code generation, using the structural regularity of programming languages to reduce output format errors.
ADELIE~\cite{qi2024adelie} uses SFT and DPO to align LLMs on IE tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results among open-source models while preserving general capabilities, though compliance with ontological constraints remains a learned soft preference rather than a hard constraint.
In the supervised setting, joint entity-relation architectures such as SpERT~\cite{eberts2020spert} and PFN~\cite{yan2021pfn} enforce type consistency implicitly through shared representations: SpERT classifies entity spans and relation pairs in a single BERT pass with span-level negative sampling, while PFN decomposes feature encoding into entity-specific, relation-specific, and shared partitions via gating mechanisms.
These models achieve strong performance but are limited to fixed, predefined schemas and cannot generalize to unseen ontologies without retraining, precisely the ontology-portable scenario requiring no constraint-specific training that OntoCoDec targets.
EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} applies Answer Set Programming (ASP) constraints during decoding of joint entity-relation extraction models, enforcing structural type compatibility at generation time. This is a decoding-time approach, though with model-specific, manually authored constraints rather than ontology-driven compilation.
Training-based methods provide \emph{soft} structural guidance: the model learns to prefer valid outputs but cannot enforce compliance at inference time, as demonstrated by non-trivial violation rates even in fine-tuned systems.
Importantly, training-based and decoding-time approaches are complementary rather than competing: a system like GoLLIE could be combined with OntoCoDec's constraint layers, using fine-tuning to maximize the probability of valid outputs while decoding-time enforcement eliminates residual violations.
OntoCoDec provides \emph{hard} decoding-time enforcement that requires no constraint-specific training, is automatically compiled from IE ontologies, and composable with any of these training-based approaches.

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 4: Type-Checking / Ontology Validation
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Post-hoc Ontology Validation.}
Rather than constraining generation, several methods validate LLM outputs against ontological rules after generation, applying a detect-then-fix paradigm.
ODKE+~\cite{khorshidi2025odke} dynamically generates ontology snippets containing domain/range constraints as prompt context, achieving 98.8\% precision across 195 predicates at web scale, but constraint adherence relies on prompt-level guidance, not enforcement, leaving residual violations unaddressed.
SPIRES/OntoGPT~\cite{spires_2024} provides an ontology-based extraction framework that grounds LLM outputs against OBO ontologies post-generation: it validates extracted entities and relations through ontology lookup and corrects mismatches in a second pass, the prompt-then-validate paradigm in the biomedical domain.
OntoLogX~\cite{ontologx_2025} applies SHACL validation to LLM-generated knowledge graphs, iteratively re-prompting the LLM to correct constraint violations and reducing them by approximately 10$\times$ across multiple correction rounds. This demonstrates the detect-then-fix paradigm's effectiveness but also its inherent multi-pass cost.
\citet{upadhyay2023openie} inject entity-type knowledge as constraints into Open IE via both constrained inference and constraint-aware training, improving F1 by 29\% on CaRB, though their constrained inference operates over a discrete candidate set rather than during autoregressive generation.
\citet{regino2025kgcurator} propose a multi-stage LLM pipeline for validating RDF triple insertions against RDFS domain/range constraints, where each validation step requires a separate LLM call, effective but computationally expensive at scale.
RELATE~\cite{olasunkanmi2025relate} addresses the alignment gap between LLM-extracted biomedical relations and standardized ontology predicates through a three-stage pipeline: ontology preprocessing with predicate embeddings, similarity-based retrieval via SapBERT, and LLM-based reranking with negation handling, achieving 94\% accuracy@10 on ChemProt.
While RELATE demonstrates effective ontology grounding for relation extraction, its constraints are applied \emph{post-extraction} through retrieval and reranking rather than during generation, and it requires domain-specific embedding models trained on biomedical corpora.
OntoCoDec enforces ontology constraints \emph{during} autoregressive decoding and requires no additional trained components beyond the base LLM.
Concurrently, \citet{zhou2026ontologytools} compile OWL ontologies into executable tool interfaces within The World Avatar framework; LLM agents must invoke ontology-aware tools that enforce semantic constraints during knowledge graph construction from scientific text.
This ``ontology-to-tools'' approach shares OntoCoDec's philosophy of compiling formal ontological knowledge into runtime enforcement mechanisms, but operates at the tool-call level (constraining which API functions the agent invokes) rather than at the token level (constraining which tokens the decoder produces), and requires an agentic multi-step workflow rather than single-pass autoregressive generation.
\citet{ekaw2024_ontology_beam} introduce ontology-constrained beam scoring for clinical summarization, applying soft biases (not hard masks) during beam search to steer outputs toward ontology-compliant terms, a middle ground between unconstrained generation and hard enforcement that reduces but cannot eliminate violations.
Post-hoc validation detects violations after generation and requires rejection or correction cycles that waste compute. In our setting, 15.37\% of generated triples contain domain/range violations under unconstrained decoding, a substantial waste of generation effort.
OntoCoDec \emph{prevents} violations during decoding, redirecting probability mass to valid alternatives rather than discarding invalid outputs, with only marginal overhead from logits masking compared to the cost of regenerating or correcting violated triples.
Soft-constraint approaches such as ontology-weighted beam scoring reduce violation frequency but cannot eliminate it, whereas OntoCoDec substantially reduces violations (DR$\downarrow$94\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$45--90\% on DocRED depending on model).

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 5: Constrained Decoding Quality Concerns
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Quality Impact of Constrained Decoding.}
A growing body of work raises concerns that constrained decoding degrades LLM generation quality, particularly for reasoning-intensive tasks where format enforcement interferes with chain-of-thought processes.
\citet{tam2024letmespeak} conduct a comprehensive evaluation showing that rigid format constraints (JSON, XML) harm performance on math and multi-hop QA benchmarks but \emph{benefit} classification-style tasks such as slot filling, a distinction directly relevant to IE, which is fundamentally an extraction (classification-like) task rather than a reasoning task.
CRANE~\cite{banerjee2025crane} provides theoretical analysis of why restricting outputs to narrow grammars suppresses chain-of-thought reasoning by eliminating intermediate reasoning tokens, and proposes an alternating strategy between unconstrained reasoning phases and constrained output phases to mitigate this effect.
\citet{schall2025hiddencost} conduct a systematic study across 11 models and multiple benchmarks, finding 10--30\% semantic correctness degradation on reasoning tasks under structural constraints, with larger models showing greater absolute degradation.
\citet{zhou2026snowballing} identify ``structure snowballing,'' a failure mode where format compliance cognitive load traps models in repetitive structural patterns rather than improving reasoning during self-correction iterations.
These findings establish a legitimate concern for constrained decoding in reasoning-heavy applications.
However, information extraction occupies a fundamentally different regime: the model extracts entities and relations from input text rather than generating novel reasoning chains, and \citet{tam2024letmespeak}'s own results show that extraction-style tasks are robust to, or even benefit from, format constraints.
OntoCoDec addresses this concern empirically: domain/range violations decrease by 94\% on SciERC (15.37\%$\to$0.93\%) and 45--90\% on DocRED across two models, with F1-neutral impact on SciERC ($+$0.13pp, $p{=}0.58$) and significant R-F1 gains on DocRED (Qwen $p{<}0.001$, Llama $p{=}0.013$).
Critically, OntoCoDec's constraints target only type tokens (entity types, relation labels), leaving free-text spans (entity surface forms and their boundaries) entirely unconstrained, which minimizes the distribution distortion that causes quality degradation in reasoning tasks.
A two-pass variant (S2), explored in ablation (Section~5), separates extraction and constraint enforcement into distinct passes, analogous to CRANE's alternating strategy; however, our primary single-pass approach already avoids reasoning interference by constraining only type tokens while leaving free-text spans unconstrained.

% ===========================================================================
% Our Approach
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Our Approach.}
OntoCoDec occupies a unique position in this landscape: it is the first system to \emph{automatically compile} IE ontologies, including domain/range axioms, into token-level semantic masks, extending grammar-constrained decoding from syntactic to semantic enforcement without manually authored rules.
Unlike vocabulary-constrained methods that restrict individual tokens to a fixed set, OntoCoDec enforces \emph{cross-field relational constraints} through a stateful entity registry that tracks extracted types during autoregressive generation; constraint evaluation is dynamic and depends on previously decoded content.
This approach is orthogonal to supervised IE methods and applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access without model modification or additional training (evaluated on 7B--70B models across three tokenizer families).
Unlike training-based IE systems, OntoCoDec requires no constraint-specific training and substantially reduces type violations at inference time (DR$\downarrow$94\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$45--90\% on DocRED); unlike post-hoc validation, it prevents violations rather than detecting them, redirecting probability mass to valid alternatives with significant R-F1 gains on DocRED ($p \leq 0.013$) and F1-neutral impact on SciERC.
The two constraint layers, grammar (structural) and semantic (relational), compose via bitwise AND with a scale-dependent interaction: the grammar layer ensures every generated type token belongs to the valid vocabulary, which enables the semantic layer to look up and enforce domain/range rules for that type.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user is operating as a Director managing an AI Research Reviewer agent (me) for the `schema_semantic_constrained_ie` project. This is Loop #20 of the Reviewer session. The project is an EMNLP 2026 paper (OntoCoDec: Type-Constrained Information Extraction via Compiled Schema Constraints) in submission-ready state, targeting May 25 ARR deadline (~36h away). The Director triggered a series of systematic pre-submission reviews:
   - Claim strength audit of abstract/intro
   - Body claim calibration + Limitations review
   - References format audit (67 bib entries)
   - Strategic story review with EMNLP scoring prediction
   - Novelty defense analysis (most recent, was in progress)

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **OntoCoDec**: Two-layer constrained decoding framework for IE (grammar layer via XGrammar + semantic layer via dynamic entity registry + logit masking)
   - **Violation types**: DR (domain/range), RV (relation vocabulary), ET (entity type), CF (cross-field consistency)
   - **Non-additive composition**: Grammar alone 3% DR reduction, semantic alone 24%, combined 94% — the paper's "central empirical finding"
   - **Scale-dependent layer interaction**: At 70B, semantic layer independently achieves 84% DR reduction vs 24% at 8B
   - **Decidability taxonomy**: Three levels — (1) context-free, (2) prefix-decidable with state, (3) non-local
   - **S1 vs S2 strategies**: S1 (single-pass, recommended) vs S2 (two-pass, S2 over-constrains at 70B causing -8pp R-F1)
   - **Beam search**: k=2 Pareto-optimal, k=4 eliminates all violations at 8B
   - **Tot calculation**: DR+CF only (not RV/ET), because under S1 RV=ET=0
   - **EMNLP 2026 ARR scoring**: 5=Award, 4=Conference, 3=Findings, 2=Resubmit
   - **PICARD differentiation**: SQL types are statically declared; IE entity types are inferred during generation requiring dynamic registry

3. Files and Code Sections:

C1=empirical ablation, C2=two-layer framework + decidability, C3=preliminary 70B scale exploration. Key weakness: C1 leads with "systematic ablation" (sounds incremental), non-additive composition not explicitly in contribution list.

Issues found: 7 orphan entries, author format inconsistency in 4 entries, 2 entries with "and others" (luo2025kgtrie, vukovic2024dialogue), 1 abbreviated booktitle (wadden2019entity), ICLR venue 4 variants.

% New citations for schema_semantic_constrained_ie
% Generated 2026-05-18
% All entries moved to relwork_new_entries.bib; this file kept empty to avoid duplicate key errors.

% §5 Setup (compressed from Violation Landscape)
% exp_ids: mvp_phase0_violation_rate, mvp_phase0_scierc_schema,
%          mvp_phase0_violation_rate_docred, mvp_phase0_docred_schema

\label{sec:violation_landscape}

We evaluate OntoCoDec in two deployment configurations: greedy S1 (DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, $+$10\% latency) and beam S1 (all violations\,$\to$\,0\%, 1.39$\times$ latency); zero-shot evaluation (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}) serves as a diagnostic probe for the fine-tuned setting (R-F1 40--46\%).

\paragraph{Setup.}
We evaluate on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) and DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 development documents; test annotations are not publicly available; 96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$).
RE type constraints are extracted from observed type pairs in training data (neither dataset provides a formal ontology); EE constraints on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}) derive from the KAIROS ontology.
All constraints are schema-level, independent of evaluation splits.
Primary model: Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, zero-shot greedy decoding; cross-model validation in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}, composability with fine-tuning in \S\ref{sec:composability}.
LoRA hyperparameters (rank, $\alpha$, learning rate) were tuned on SciERC and transferred to DocRED without dataset-specific optimization; given the substantial schema complexity difference (7 vs.\ 96 relations), this transfer may underestimate DocRED fine-tuning potential.
Our R-F1 range (40--46\% under LoRA) is consistent with recent LLM-based generative RE evaluations on these benchmarks, where document-level closed IE without gold entity spans typically achieves 35--50\%~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}; supervised span-based methods operating under different assumptions (gold entity spans, dedicated architectures) are not directly comparable.
For reference, the supervised end-to-end SOTA on SciERC achieves 41.6\% strict Rel-F1 (PL-Marker~\cite{ye2022packed}) and 36.8\% (PURE~\cite{zhong2021frustratingly}); while evaluation protocols differ, our 40--46\% R-F1 range under LoRA falls within a comparable band.
DocRED development documents were used for evaluation only.
Four violation categories: \textbf{DR} (type pair $\notin \sigma(r)$), \textbf{RV} (relation $\notin \mathcal{R}$), \textbf{ET} (entity type $\notin \mathcal{E}$), \textbf{CF} (conflicting types across triples).
Baseline DR: 15.37\% (SciERC), 18.46\% (DocRED); schema-informed prompting reduces DR by 62\% but is per-relation unreliable (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).

% Runtime overhead (inline paragraph, no subsection header to save space)

\paragraph{Runtime overhead.}
\label{sec:runtime}
S1 overhead is $+$13.1\% on SciERC, lower on DocRED due to amortization over longer sequences; under LoRA, $+$10.0\% with 37\% lower absolute latency.
Constraint compilation is one-time $<$0.5\,s; scaling benchmarks confirm constant overhead (2--3\%) up to 200 entity types and 1{,}000 relations (Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}).

\paragraph{Beam search compatibility.}
\label{sec:beam-results}
% exp_id: d066_beam_sweep
With LoRA, beam search~\cite{anderson2017guided} eliminates all four violation types at 8B on both SciERC and DocRED; at 70B, beam $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$RV${=}$ET${=}$0\% with one residual CF on SciERC (Appendix~\ref{app:beam-search}).
A beam-width sweep ($k \in \{1,2,4,8\}$) on SciERC reveals $k{=}2$ as Pareto-optimal: R-F1 44.60 (highest), CF 0.11\%, at only 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency; $k{=}4$ achieves CF${=}$0\% but lower R-F1 (43.60) at 1.39$\times$ (Table~\ref{tab:beam-sweep}; latencies relative to greedy S1).
This yields three deployment tiers: greedy S1 ($+$10\% latency, DR${\leq}$0.21\%, CF${\leq}$1.4\%), beam $k{=}2$ (1.18$\times$, near-zero CF), and beam $k{=}4$ (1.39$\times$, all violations${\to}$0\% at 8B).
Per-beam memory overhead is $O(k \times |\text{entities}| \times |\text{types}|)$ for independent entity registry copies, negligible at typical document scales.

% exp_ids: r16_70b_scierc_zs_s1, r16_70b_docred_zs_s1, 70b_lora_scierc, 70b_lora_docred_200
\paragraph{70B-class validation (single-family).}
\label{sec:70b-results}
The following results constitute a preliminary single-family scale exploration on Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (AWQ INT4); cross-family verification (e.g., Qwen-72B) remains future work.
All 70B experiments use Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct under AWQ INT4 quantization; an 8B ablation confirms constraint enforcement is unaffected by quantization (Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).
Zero-shot S1 eliminates DR on both datasets (SciERC 6.41\%\,$\to$\,0\%, DocRED 14.98\%\,$\to$\,0\%; R-F1 11--13).
% exp_ids: r16_70b_scierc_zs_ablation (grammar_only, semantic_only, full_s1)
A four-way ablation reveals scale-dependent layer interaction: semantic-only achieves 84\% DR reduction vs.\ 8B's 24\% (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}), though grammar remains necessary for RV elimination and CF control (semantic-only CF${=}$76).
% exp_ids: eval_70b_lora_scierc_s1_constrained, eval_70b_lora_docred_200_s1_constrained
LoRA confirms composability: DR\,$\to$\,0\% on both datasets (R-F1 44.53, 43.95; $|\Delta| \leq 0.20$\,pp; CF 0.18--1.33\%); cross-family generalization at 70B scale remains to be verified.
% exp_ids: eval_70b_lora_docred_200_beam4_s1
Beam ($k{=}4$) reduces DocRED parse failures (12.5\%\,$\to$\,0.5\%, R-F1 $+$4.19\,pp); SciERC controlled comparison isolates pure beam gain at $+$0.28\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:70b-ablation}).

% exp_ids: trie_qwen_ft_scierc, trie_qwen_zs_scierc, trie_llama_ft_scierc, trie_llama_zs_scierc
\paragraph{Comparison with grammar-constrained approaches.}
\label{sec:constrained-baselines}
Our grammar-only ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation}, row~2) implements the same constraints as GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} and BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025}; vLLM \texttt{guided\_json}~\cite{kwon2023vllm} confirms equivalence on Qwen3-8B (DR${=}$15.26\%; other models use the same backend; Appendix~\ref{app:gcd-comparison}).
The ${\sim}$15\% residual DR is the gap our semantic layer addresses (94\% total reduction); trie-only constraints without JSON enforcement yield 9--51\% parse failure (Appendix~\ref{app:trie-baseline}).

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 2 RE datasets (SciERC, DocRED) and 3 model families, with a preliminary event extraction pilot (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
The central empirical finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
We offer a speculative hypothesis: larger models exhibit improved vocabulary calibration, assigning higher probability to ontology-valid tokens and reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}); confirming this causal mechanism requires cross-family verification beyond our current scope.
Supporting evidence includes the fallback frequency gap: under LoRA + S1, Qwen-8B triggers 0 grammar-first fallbacks on SciERC while Llama-8B triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), yet both achieve DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, confirming that fallback frequency does not determine enforcement effectiveness.
Grammar-constrained decoding is thus necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Net effect: total violations (DR+CF) decrease 30--51\% in zero-shot and 26--52\% under fine-tuned greedy S1; beam $k{=}4$ eliminates all. DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR).
S2 (two-pass) exhibits scale-sensitive behavior: comparable to S1 at 8B but $-$8\,pp R-F1 at 70B, consistent with CRANE's~\cite{banerjee2025crane} finding that aggressive constraint enforcement can interfere with well-calibrated reasoning; we recommend S1 as the default configuration.

\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability}); global entity-level type consensus exceeds online per-token masking.
Beam search and TCR approximate this; integrating consensus into decoding remains future work.

[severity: warning] Novelty 防御力审查 — Intro Framing 对 A1 攻击面的防御

A1（"已知技术组合，非新颖"）是本文最危险的攻击面。当前 intro framing 存在 4 个可零成本修复的弱点：

---

**1. 贡献列表未包含论文最独特的发现**

§7 conclusion 明确称 non-additive layer interaction 为 "the central empirical finding"（grammar 3% + semantic 24% → composed 94%），但贡献列表 C1-C3 中**完全没有提及**。C1 以 "Systematic ablation" 开头，听起来像增量工作而非洞察。

建议 C1 改写：
- 当前：「A systematic ablation across five constraint configurations...」
- 建议：「An empirical finding of non-additive layer interaction: grammar-only constraints reduce domain-range violations by 3% and semantic-only by 24%, but their composition achieves 94%—revealing an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.」

**2. C2 措辞被动/弱化**

- 当前：「...grounded in the observation that IE constraints span three decidability levels」
- 建议：「A decidability analysis showing that IE constraints span three levels—context-free, prefix-decidable with state, and non-local—and that the first two are enforceable during generation via compiled token masks.」

"grounded in the observation" 是被动叙述；"showing" 是主动发现。审稿人读前者会觉得"别人也能观察到"，读后者会觉得"这是你的分析贡献"。

**3. C3 以 "Preliminary" 开头，直接信号弱点**

- 当前：「Preliminary evidence that constraint effectiveness scales with model size...」
- 建议：「Evidence of scale-dependent layer interaction: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84% DR reduction (vs. 24% at 8B)...」

"Preliminary" 是审稿人最喜欢的攻击词——作者自己都说是 preliminary，凭什么接收？70B 结果覆盖两个数据集 + LoRA composability，已超出 "preliminary" 的范畴。

**4. 主文 §6 Related Work 中 PICARD 区分严重不足**

主文 §6 仅用 2 句泛泛提及 PICARD，没有点出核心区别。但 appendix_related_work.tex 第 22-33 行有**极好的区分**：

> "PICARD operates over a fixed, fully enumerated schema where column types are statically declared... OntoCoDec's entity registry is populated during generation as entity spans are extracted from free text, requiring prefix-decidable enforcement (Level 2) rather than context-free lookup."

建议将这 1-2 句核心区分（static declared types vs. dynamic inferred types）提入主文 §6 的 PICARD 句子中。这是零成本的 novelty 强化——审稿人看主文不看 appendix，当前主文完全没有传达出与 PICARD 的本质差异。

---

**总结**：当前 intro 将贡献 frame 为 "工程性工作+系统评估"，但论文的真正价值在于 (a) non-additive composition 这一反直觉发现，(b) decidability 分析提供的理论 grounding，(c) 70B scale interaction 的实证。上述 4 个零成本改写可将 framing 从 "engineering" 转向 "insight/finding"，直接缓解 A1 攻击面。

附带提醒：主文 WikiEvents 段落称 "preliminary n=20 pilot"，但 appendix 实际有 246-doc × 3-model 的完整 ZS 结果。这也在不经意间弱化了方法的泛化性证据，建议更新措辞。

- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.

    prompt 级干预不足以解决问题后正式宣布 MVP 通过。'

  rationale: Phase 0 三个实验完成：SciERC 15.4%/5.78%, DocRED 18.7% domain_range violation

    路径可用，S2 bug 修复中）。cuda:1 空闲，立即启动 Phase 2 SciERC grammar_only/semantic_only/full_s1
    实验。
  related_experiments:
  - exp_id: mvp_phase0_violation_rate
    role: primary
    result: SciERC DR=15.4%, GO
  - exp_id: mvp_phase0_scierc_schema
    role: primary
    result: SciERC DR=5.78%, prompt insufficient
  - exp_id: mvp_phase0_violation_rate_docred
    role: primary
    result: DocRED DR=18.7%, GO
  depends_on:
  - D002
- id: D004
  date: 2026-05-14 01:53 UTC
  summary: Phase 2 SciERC 核心结果确认：grammar+semantic (full_s1) DR↓94% F1 neutral，两层约束协同效应成立
  rationale: _v2 干净数据 551 样本全量结果：full_s1 DR=0.93%（baseline 15.37%，↓94%），R-F1 微升 +0.0013。grammar
    单独消除 RV/ET，semantic 单独降 DR 24%，组合后 94%——超加性效应。论文核心 claim 站住。早期污染数据 semantic_only
    DR=16.43% 已修正为 11.65%。
  related_experiments:
  - exp_id: phase2_scierc_unconstrained
    role: baseline
    result: DR=15.37%
  - exp_id: phase2_scierc_grammar_only
    role: ablation
    result: DR=14.84%, RV/ET=0%
  - exp_id: phase2_scierc_semantic_only
    role: ablation
    result: DR=11.65%
  - exp_id: phase2_scierc_full_s1
    role: core_result
    result: DR=0.93%, F1=0.0836
  depends_on:
  - D003
- id: D005
  date: 2026-05-14 01:53 UTC
  summary: Phase 2 SciERC 核心结果确认：Full S1 DR↓94% F1无损，CF violation↑124x 作为已知 tradeoff
    待 S2 对比后决定处理策略

2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec along three axes.
5	
6	\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
7	XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, SynCode~\cite{ugare2024syncode}, SGLang~\cite{zheng2024sglang}, and related systems~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql,park2024grammar,jsonschemabench2025} enforce format validity via CFG-based token masking but lack cross-field semantic awareness.
8	PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile type systems into prefix automata; KG-Trie~\cite{luo2025kgtrie} applies trie-based KG constraints during decoding for knowledge-to-text generation.
9	Unlike PICARD, which operates over a fixed, fully enumerated SQL schema with statically declared column types, OntoCoDec's entity registry is populated dynamically during generation as entity spans are extracted from free text, requiring prefix-decidable enforcement rather than context-free lookup.
10	
11	\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
12	GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}, and others~\cite{guidex2025,josifoski2022genie,paolini2021tanl,cabot2021rebel,wang2023instructuie,qi2024adelie,fei2022lasuie,lu2022uie,zhou2024universalner} encode ontology structure via training-time internalization without runtime enforcement~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.

14	
15	\paragraph{Constraint enforcement in IE.}
16	\citet{roth_yih_2004} and \citet{riedel2010modeling} formulated hard type constraints via ILP; post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025} detects violations after generation but discards up to 74\% of predictions.

18	Grammar-only enforcement (GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd}, BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025}) achieves only 3\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:constrained-baselines}).
19

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); 97.6--100\% of removed triples are false positives (\S\ref{sec:downstream-impact}). Beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets (${\sim}$1.5$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations (DR+CF) decreasing 30--51\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item An empirical finding of non-additive layer interaction: grammar-only constraints reduce domain-range violations by 3\% and semantic-only by 24\%, but their composition achieves 94\%---revealing an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework showing that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars---grammar-only approaches face state spaces of $6^{17}$--$6^{19}$ for typical IE schemas (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Evidence of scale-dependent layer interaction on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4): the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

1	% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion
2	
3	OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 2 RE datasets (SciERC, DocRED) and 3 model families, with event extraction validation (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
4	The central empirical finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.
5	
6	\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
7	This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
8	We offer a speculative hypothesis: larger models exhibit improved vocabulary calibration, assigning higher probability to ontology-valid tokens and reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}); confirming this causal mechanism requires cross-family verification beyond our current scope.
9	Supporting evidence includes the fallback frequency gap: under LoRA + S1, Qwen-8B triggers 0 grammar-first fallbacks on SciERC while Llama-8B triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), yet both achieve DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, confirming that fallback frequency does not determine enforcement effectiveness.
10	Grammar-constrained decoding is thus necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).
11	
12	\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
13	Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
14	Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
15	Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
16	Net effect: total violations (DR+CF) decrease 30--51\% in zero-shot and 26--52\% under fine-tuned greedy S1; beam $k{=}4$ eliminates all. DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
17	
18	\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
19	GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR).
20	S2 (two-pass) exhibits scale-sensitive behavior: comparable to S1 at 8B but $-$8\,pp R-F1 at 70B, consistent with CRANE's~\cite{banerjee2025crane} finding that aggressive constraint enforcement can interfere with well-calibrated reasoning; we recommend S1 as the default configuration.
21	
22	\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
23	Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability}); global entity-level type consensus exceeds online per-token masking.
24	Beam search and TCR approximate this; integrating consensus into decoding remains future work.
25

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 2 RE datasets (SciERC, DocRED) and 3 model families, with event extraction validation (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
The central empirical finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
We offer a speculative hypothesis: larger models exhibit improved vocabulary calibration, assigning higher probability to ontology-valid tokens and reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}); confirming this causal mechanism requires cross-family verification beyond our current scope.
Supporting evidence includes the fallback frequency gap: under LoRA + S1, Qwen-8B triggers 0 grammar-first fallbacks on SciERC while Llama-8B triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), yet both achieve DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, confirming that fallback frequency does not determine enforcement effectiveness.
Grammar-constrained decoding is thus necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Net effect: total violations (DR+CF) decrease 30--51\% in zero-shot and 26--52\% under fine-tuned greedy S1; beam $k{=}4$ eliminates all. DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR).
S2 (two-pass) exhibits scale-sensitive behavior: comparable to S1 at 8B but $-$8\,pp R-F1 at 70B, consistent with CRANE's~\cite{banerjee2025crane} finding that aggressive constraint enforcement can interfere with well-calibrated reasoning; we recommend S1 as the default configuration.

\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability}); global entity-level type consensus exceeds online per-token masking.
Beam search and TCR approximate this; integrating consensus into decoding remains future work.

These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).

We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles information extraction ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry.

4	\label{sec:wikievents}
